params.question: The case describes that a glottic tumour carries a better prognosis than a supraglottic tumour at the same stage. What anatomical factor primarily accounts for this difference?

answers.text: Glottic tumours are typically smaller at diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Size at diagnosis does not explain the prognostic difference. The key factor is the pattern of lymphatic drainage, which differs sharply between the two regions.

answers.text: The pattern of lymphatic drainage differs between the two regions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The supraglottis has rich bilateral lymphatic drainage enabling early nodal spread, while the glottis has very sparse lymphatics, making metastasis rare.

answers.text: The supraglottic mucosa is thinner, allowing deeper tumour invasion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mucosal thickness is not the key determinant. The critical difference lies in lymphatic drainage — abundant in the supraglottis, virtually absent in the glottis.

answers.text: The blood supply to the glottis is more limited, slowing tumour growth

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Blood supply does not primarily explain this prognostic gap. The answer lies in lymphatic drainage: rich and bilateral in the supraglottis, nearly absent at the true vocal cords.

overallFeedback.feedback: The critical difference is lymphatic drainage. The supraglottis has abundant bilateral lymphatics enabling early nodal metastasis. The true vocal cords have virtually no lymphatics, so glottic cancers rarely spread, resulting in a much better prognosis.

Correct! Lymphatic drainage is the key anatomical factor. The supraglottis drains to bilateral cervical nodes, so tumours spread early. The true vocal cords have almost no lymphatics, giving glottic cancers an excellent prognosis.

interactions.label: Why is the subglottis the most vulnerable site for airway obstruction in young c

params.question: Why is the subglottis the most vulnerable site for airway obstruction in young children?

answers.text: The aryepiglottic folds are proportionally larger in children, narrowing the passage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The aryepiglottic folds form the lateral edges of the laryngeal inlet, not the subglottic airway. The subglottis is bounded by the rigid cricoid cartilage.

answers.text: The cricoid cartilage forms a rigid, inelastic ring that cannot expand to accommodate swelling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The cricoid is the only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway. In children, the subglottis is the narrowest point, so even mild oedema within this inelastic ring causes significant obstruction.

answers.text: The rima glottidis is narrower in children, creating a bottleneck at the subglottic level

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In adults, the rima glottidis is the narrowest point. But in children, the subglottis at the cricoid ring is narrower — this is why croup causes stridor in children but not usually in adults.

answers.text: The subglottic mucosa in children lacks protective respiratory epithelium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The subglottis does have respiratory epithelium. The vulnerability comes from the rigid cricoid ring, which is the only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway and cannot expand.

overallFeedback.feedback: In children, the subglottis — bounded by the rigid, inelastic cricoid cartilage — is the narrowest part of the airway. Even mild mucosal swelling within this unyielding complete ring causes significant obstruction, the anatomical basis of stridor in croup.

Correct! The cricoid is the only complete ring in the respiratory tract and cannot expand. In children, this makes the subglottis the narrowest airway segment, explaining why conditions like croup cause stridor with only mild oedema.

interactions.label: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch of the aorta before asc

params.question: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch of the aorta before ascending to the larynx.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The LEFT recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch; the RIGHT loops under the right subclavian artery. The left nerve's longer course through the chest makes it more vulnerable to mediastinal pathology such as aortic aneurysm or lung apex tumours.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. It is the LEFT recurrent laryngeal nerve that loops under the aortic arch at the ligamentum arteriosum, giving it a longer intrathoracic course. The RIGHT nerve loops under the right subclavian artery.

params.question: During thyroid surgery, the recurrent laryngeal nerve is most at risk because of its variable anatomical relationship with which structure?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The superior thyroid artery relates to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, not the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The RLN crosses the inferior thyroid artery.

Correct! The recurrent laryngeal nerve crosses the inferior thyroid artery, and this relationship is highly variable — anterior in about half, posterior in a third, and between its branches in the remainder.
The common carotid artery lies in the carotid sheath lateral to the thyroid gland. The RLN's critical surgical relationship is with the inferior thyroid artery, where its course is unpredictable.
The thyrocervical trunk gives rise to the inferior thyroid artery, but the nerve's critical variable crossing occurs specifically at the inferior thyroid artery itself.

overallFeedback.feedback: The recurrent laryngeal nerve crosses the inferior thyroid artery, and this relationship is variable — anterior in ~50% of cases, posterior in ~33%, and between its branches in the rest. This anatomical variability is why thyroid surgery is the most common cause of RLN injury.

Correct! The RLN crosses the inferior thyroid artery with a variable relationship: anterior in about half of cases, posterior in a third, and between branches in the remainder. This variability makes the nerve vulnerable during thyroid surgery.
